standard_prerequisites.name: The integers as a quotient of pairs
standard_prerequisites.statement: In this chapter \Z is presented as the quotient \sm{x:\N\times\N}(r(x)=x) of pairs of natural numbers by an idempotent r, so that \Z is equivalent to the usual integers.
standard_prerequisites.use: The proof works with this presentation and transports the result afterwards (source line 1416).

standard_prerequisites.name: Quotient map on the canonical representatives
standard_prerequisites.statement: The map q(x) \defeq (r(x), i(x)) is the quotient map, and q agrees on a pair and its successor pair.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the map the family is pulled back along (source lines 1417-1421).

standard_prerequisites.name: Double induction on the natural numbers
standard_prerequisites.statement: A family on \N \times \N is defined by giving its values on the two axes and on the diagonal step, together with a step for the diagonal.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the induction that constructs g (source lines 1428-1434).

core_obligations: Replace the integers by their presentation as the quotient of pairs with r(x)=x and pull the given family P back along the quotient map q to a family Q on \N \times \N (source lines 1416-1420).
Transport the three given data across the equalities that identify the base point and the two step maps to obtain d'_0, d'_+ and d'_- for Q (source lines 1421-1425).
Use q(n,m) = q(n+1,m+1) to obtain an equivalence e_{n,m} : Q(n,m) \simeq Q(n+1,m+1) (source lines 1426-1427).
Define g : \prd{x} Q(x) by double induction, with the three base and axis clauses and the diagonal clause g(n+1,m+1) \defeq e_{n,m}(g(n,m)) (source lines 1428-1434).

Push the result back along the section \proj1 of q, using Q \circ \proj1 = P and the resulting family of equivalences, to obtain f : \prd{z:\Z} P(z) with the three stated computation rules (source lines 1435-1437).

proof_roadmap.step: Move to the quotient presentation of \Z and pull P back to Q along the quotient map.
Transport the given data and get the diagonal equivalence from q(n,m) = q(n+1,m+1).
Define g on \N \times \N by double induction.
Compose with the section of the quotient map to get f on \Z and check the three rules.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the author's labelled lemma at source lines 1399-1414 (book Theorem 6.10.12): a type family P over the integers equipped with a point over 0 and step functions for the positive and the negative successor has a section whose values at 0, at n+1 and at -(n+1) are computed by the given data. The statement gives no construction, while the proof (source lines 1415-1438) has to make the two-sided induction possible at all: it passes to the quotient presentation of the integers, pulls the family back along the quotient map to a family on \N \times \N, transports the three pieces of data across the equalities that identify the base point and the two steps, derives a diagonal equivalence from the fact that a pair and its successor pair have the same quotient, and then constructs the section by a double induction on the two natural-number coordinates; finally it pushes the result back to the integers along the section of the quotient map, using that the pullback of P is Q and the resulting family of equivalences. Neither the presentation of the integers nor the diagonal equivalence appears in the statement.
